column2: From Greek skoutárion "leather shield": after the barracks of the shield-bearing guard unit; its ancient name was Chrysopolis, "golden city"
column3: In antiquity the landing on the Anatolian shore of the Bosphorus bore the name Chrysopolis, "golden city," as a dependency of Chalcedon; it is said to have earned the name as the place where the Persians' tribute gold was collected. In the last centuries of Byzantium, the guard unit stationed here, which carried leather shields (skoutárion), gave its name to the district, and in Turkish it became Üsküdar. In the Ottoman period it was the starting point of the caravans bound for Anatolia and of the pilgrimage road; the Mihrimah Sultan and Yeni Valide complexes keep that era alive.

column2: Village of the kadi: from Mehmed the Conqueror granting the town as a benefice to Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first kadi (judge); its ancient name was Chalcedon
column3: Chalcedon, founded by Megarian colonists in 685 BC, was dubbed the "land of the blind" by a Persian commander because it was settled before Byzantion yet failed to see the superiority of the opposite shore; the Council of Chalcedon met here in 451. After the conquest, Mehmed II gave the settlement to Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first kadi, and the people called it "the kadi's village." Haydarpaşa Station and Moda are the district's 19th-century heritage.

column2: Cradle stone: from the five stone posts (beş taş) Barbaros Hayreddin Pasha erected to moor his ships, or from a cradle-shaped stone
column3: In the Byzantine period the bay was called Diplokionion, "double column," after two columns standing on the shore; under the Ottomans it became the naval base of Grand Admiral Barbaros Hayreddin Pasha. Evliya Çelebi links the name to the five stone posts Barbaros had erected to moor his ships; according to another account, a stone from the cradle of Jesus was kept in the church here. Barbaros's mausoleum and Dolmabahçe Palace define the district's identity.

column2: Origin disputed: explained by Greek gála "milk" (dairy farms), by the Galatians (Celts), or by Italian calata "road down to the quay"
column3: The hill across the Golden Horn was called Sykai, "fig grove," in Byzantium, and later Galatas. Three explanations exist for the name: the dairy farms on the shore (gála), the Galatian mercenaries quartered here, or the Genoese word calata, "road descending to the quay." Galata became a Genoese colony after 1267, and its tower, built in 1348, still stands. In the Ottoman period it was the quarter of Levantine merchants and embassies.

column2: Son of the bey: from the nickname of a nobleman who lived here (a Pontic prince or the son of the Venetian envoy Gritti); Greek Pera, "the opposite shore"
column3: The Galata heights, which the Greeks called Péran, "the other side," came to be known as Beyoğlu in the 16th century because of a nobleman who built a mansion here; he is said to have been either a Pontic prince who converted to Islam or Alvise Gritti, son of the Venetian doge. In the 19th century, with its embassies, the Pera Palace and the Cadde-i Kebir (İstiklal Avenue), it became the center of Westernized life. The Tünel (1875) is among the oldest underground funiculars in the world.

column2: In front of the office of the customs emin (customs director): from the customs house at the Golden Horn harbor
column3: The quays at the mouth of the Golden Horn were the Ottoman customs post for foreign trade; the official who ran customs affairs was called the emin, and the square in front of his office took the name Eminönü. The word emin derives from Arabic amīn, "trustworthy." The Spice Bazaar, the New Mosque and the Galata Bridge are the district's Ottoman and Republican landmarks; the harbor of ancient Byzantion also lay here.

column2: From the name of the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, built by Ahmed I between 1609 and 1617; Arabic sulṭān + Aḥmad
column3: The Byzantine Hippodrome, where chariot races were held, served the Ottomans as a festival ground under the name At Meydanı (Horse Square). When the six-minaret mosque that Sultan Ahmed I commissioned from the architect Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa rose on the south side of the square, the district came to be called by his name. Hagia Sophia, the Basilica Cistern and the Obelisk stand in the same district, displaying three thousand years of the city's layers side by side.

column2: From the name of Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, standard-bearer of the Prophet Muhammad; Arabic Ayyūb (Eyüp)
column3: The grave of the Companion Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, who died during the Arab siege of 674, is said to have been discovered by Akşemseddin after the conquest; Mehmed II built a tomb and mosque here. In the Byzantine period a monastic area called Kosmidion, the district became the sacred ground where Ottoman sultans were girded with the sword. The coffeehouse frequented by Pierre Loti and the view over the Golden Horn are another face of the district; in 2017 the word Sultan was added to the district's name.

column2: Arabic fātiḥ "conqueror, opener": the title of Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror; the area around the complex he built
column3: After the conquest of 1453, Mehmed II took the title Fatih, "the Conqueror," and between 1463 and 1470 built the complex bearing his name on the site of the Church of the Holy Apostles. The district that grew around the mosque was called by this name; the administrative district established in 1928 covers the whole historic peninsula. The word fetih comes from the Arabic root f-t-ḥ, "to open."

column2: Ottoman name Makriköy, from Greek makrochōrion "long village"; changed to Bakırköy in 1925 on the basis of sound resemblance
column3: Hebdomon, at the seventh milestone of the Byzantine capital, was the palace and barracks zone where emperors were crowned. Makrochorion, which the Greeks called "long village," lived on under the Ottomans as Makriköy. In 1925, when Greek names were being replaced, the sound resemblance was exploited to give it the name Bakırköy. The Baruthane (gunpowder works), Yeşilköy (Ayastefanos) and Atatürk Airport lie within the district's borders.

column2: Turkish rendering of the Byzantine-era harbor name Kartalimen; popularly explained by the Turkish kartal, "eagle"
column3: The fishing village on the Marmara shore appears in Byzantine sources under the name Kartalimen; in Turkish the second half of the name dropped away and the name became identified with the kartal, the eagle. A Greek and Turkish village attached to Üsküdar in the Ottoman period, Kartal became a district in 1947. Aydos Castle is a Byzantine fortress captured in the reign of Orhan Gazi.

column2: Greek pán "all" + teíchos "wall": "place walled on every side"
column3: Procopius, the historian of the emperor Justinian, mentions a walled settlement on the Marmara shore called Panteichion; the name means "enclosed by walls on all sides." The village, which took the form Pendik in Turkish pronunciation, was known in the Ottoman period for its Greek fishermen. Sabiha Gökçen Airport and the shipyard are the district's present-day identity.

column2: Yellow cliff: from the yellow-colored mineral soil in the bay or from a yellow rocky bluff
column3: The village at the Black Sea end of the Bosphorus is noted by Evliya Çelebi for its yellow soil and rocks resembling a gold mine; the name comes from sarı, "yellow," and yar, "steep bank," later reshaped into yer. Known in the Ottoman period for its fishing weirs and waterside mansions, Sarıyer includes Rumeli Hisarı and the shrine of Telli Baba. The aqueducts of the Belgrade Forest carried Istanbul's water from here.

column2: From the nickname "Şişçi" of craftsmen who made skewers (şiş: kebab skewers, iron rods) here; it became a district name with the suffix -li
column3: In the 18th century a skewer-maker's mansion and its surroundings in the fields north of Beyoğlu were known as "Şişçi"; in popular speech the name turned into Şişli and was given to the district that developed at the end of the 19th century with the tram line. The Turkish word şiş derives from Old Turkic sış, "roasting spit," and has passed into the Balkan languages as well. The house where Atatürk lived in 1918–1919 is a museum.

column2: Turkish kuzgun "raven" + -cuk: from the nickname of a holy man named Kuzgun Baba who lived here at the time of the conquest
column3: The bay, called Chrysokeramos, "golden tile," in Byzantium after its church with gilded roof tiles, took the name Kuzguncuk under the Ottomans from the nickname of a dervish named Kuzgun Baba who lived here. From the 17th century onward a district where Jewish, Greek and Armenian communities lived together, it is known for its wooden houses and its trio of mosque, church and synagogue.

column2: Arabic taqsīm "distribution": from the water-distribution structure that divided the water coming from the Belgrade Forest among the districts
column3: In 1732 Mahmud I built a stone distribution structure (taksim or maksem) that apportioned the water brought from the Belgrade Forest among the neighborhoods of Beyoğlu; the square took its name from this building. The word taksim comes from the Arabic root q-s-m, "to divide," and is used under the same name in music. The Republic Monument (1928) and Gezi Park are the square's Republican-era landmarks.

column2: From the name of Güzelce Kasım Pasha, who developed the district in the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent; Arabic Qāsim, "one who distributes"
column3: The shipyard district on the northern shore of the Golden Horn grew up around the mosque and bathhouse built in the 1530s by Güzelce Kasım Pasha, a vizier of Süleyman the Magnificent. Because the Ottoman navy's Imperial Arsenal (Tersane-i Âmire) and the office of the Kaptan Pasha were here, the district was the home of seafarers; the expression "Kasımpaşalı" reflects this tradition. The name Kasım comes from the Arabic root q-s-m.

column2: Turkish top "cannon" + Persian hāne "house, workshop": the site of the Ottoman state's cannon foundry
column3: The cannon foundry that Mehmed II established outside the Galata walls immediately after the conquest was enlarged in the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent and named the Tophane-i Âmire. The district was called after the foundry; the Kılıç Ali Pasha Mosque and the Nusretiye Mosque are the Ottoman buildings on the shore. The element hane appears in the same construction in the names Darphane (mint), Baruthane (gunpowder works) and Tersane (shipyard).

column2: Turkish boğaz "throat; narrow passage"; Greek Bósporos "ox-ford" (the legend of Io)
column3: In Greek legend the waterway swum across by Io, whom Zeus had turned into a cow, was named Bosporos, "ox-ford"; Herodotus describes the bridge of boats that the Persian king Darius had built across it. In Turkish the word boğaz means both the bodily organ and a narrow sea passage, and comes from Old Turkic boguz; in Ottoman usage Boğaziçi denoted the waterside mansions and villages on both shores. The Rumeli and Anadolu fortresses are the two locks of the strait.

column2: Arabic ḫalīc "gulf, inlet"; famous under the Greek name Chrysokeras, "Golden Horn"
column3: The deep inlet that makes Byzantion a peninsula was named Chrysokeras, "Golden Horn," by the Greeks for its horn-like shape and rich fisheries; the Golden Horn of European languages is a translation of this name. The Ottomans used the Arabic word ḫalīc, "gulf," as a proper name. The hauling of ships overland and down into the inlet in 1453 is the famous scene of the conquest narratives; the shipyard and the Fener-Balat waterfront are the inlet's two shores.

column2: Turkish "big island": the largest of the Princes' Islands; Greek Prinkipo, "prince's island"
column3: In the Byzantine period the island to which exiled empresses and princes were confined in monasteries was called Prinkipos, "prince's island"; the name Princes' Islands for the whole archipelago comes from this. In Turkish the island's size became its name outright. Filled in the 19th century with the wooden mansions of Greek and Levantine summer residents, the island was Trotsky's place of exile between 1929 and 1933. The Monastery of Aya Yorgi (St. George) stands on its summit.

column2: Greek kallí- "beautiful" + pólis "city": "beautiful city"
column3: The harbor town at the narrowest point of the Thracian Chersonese bore the Greek name Kallipolis, "beautiful city." Süleyman Pasha's capture in 1354 of the fortress, which had been wrecked by an earthquake, marks the beginning of the Ottoman crossing into Rumelia; the name, Gelibolu in Turkish pronunciation, preserves the element -polis. It was the first base of the Ottoman navy and the birthplace of Pîrî Reis; the Gallipoli campaign of 1915 is known by the peninsula's name.

column2: Turkish boğaz "narrow passage" + Çanakkale; Greek Hellespontos, "sea of Helle"; in Western languages the Dardanelles (from the city of Dardanos)
column3: According to legend, the waterway in which Helle drowned after falling from the back of the golden-fleeced ram was called Hellespontos, "sea of Helle"; the Persian king Xerxes crossed it by a bridge of boats in 480 BC. The Dardanelles of Western languages comes from the name of the ancient city of Dardanos on the Asian shore. The Turkish name is taken from the town of Çanakkale at the strait's narrowest point. In 1915 the Allied fleet that tried to force the strait was halted here.

column2: From the names Wiluša (Ilion) and Taruiša (Troy) in Hittite texts; the city of Homer's Iliad
column3: The nine-layered mound on the hill of Hisarlık is identified with the city of the Trojan War recounted in Homer's Iliad; the kingdom of Wiluša in western Anatolia and the place name Taruiša in Hittite documents are matched with the Greek names Ilion and Troia. Heinrich Schliemann began excavating here in 1870. The Turkish form Truva comes from the French pronunciation Troie, while Troya comes directly from Greek. The legend of the wooden horse has given the world's languages the expression "Trojan horse."

column2: Turkish boz "gray, barren" + -ca + ada "island": "grayish island"; its ancient name was Tenedos
column3: Tenedos, mentioned by Homer, is the island where the Greeks hid their ships during the Trojan War; it takes its name from the legend of Tenes. When the island joined the Ottoman realm in the reign of Mehmed II, the Turks called it Bozcaada because of its arid appearance; Venice held the island briefly in 1656. On this island, known for its viticulture and its castle, Greek and Turkish cultures lived side by side for centuries.

column2: Turkish gökçe "bluish, beautiful" + ada "island"; until 1970 İmroz, from the ancient name Imbros
column3: Imbros in the northern Aegean appears in Homer as the island where Poseidon kept his horses; in Ottoman documents it is written İmroz. The island, which remained in Turkey under the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, received the name Gökçeada in 1970. The word gökçe derives from the Old Turkic root kök, "blue"; it is Turkey's largest island and is known for its organic farming.

column2: Name of the city of Assos, founded by colonists from Lesbos; the Ottoman village Behramkale, from the castle of a bey named Behram
column3: Assos, founded in the 7th century BC by colonists from the island of Lesbos, is the city where Aristotle taught philosophy for three years; the Temple of Athena stands on the summit with its andesite columns. The village's Turkish name, Behramkale, is linked to Behram Bey, who repaired the castle here in the 14th century; the Hüdavendigâr Mosque dates from the same period. The name Assos belongs to the region's pre-Greek language.

column2: From the name of Nikaia, wife of Lysimachus; İznik from the Greek phrase "eis Nikaian" (to Nicaea)
column3: Lysimachus, a general of Alexander the Great, gave the city the name of his wife Nikaia in 301 BC; the First Council of Nicaea in 325 fixed the Christian creed here. Between 1081 and 1097 it was the first capital of the Anatolian Seljuks; Orhan Gazi took the city in 1331 and founded the first Ottoman madrasa here. The Greek phrase "eis Nikaian" became İznik in Turkish. The İznik tiles of the 16th century are the summit of Ottoman art.

column2: Italian Montagna and Turkish Mudanya renderings of Apameia, named after Apama, wife of the Bithynian king Prusias I
column3: Myrleia, founded by colonists from Colophon, was renamed Apameia by the Bithynian king Prusias I after his wife Apama. The harbor, written Montagna in Genoese and Venetian portolan charts, became Mudanya in Turkish. In the town, which served as Bursa's port, the Armistice of Mudanya was signed on October 11, 1922; it is known for its silk and olive trade.

column2: Turkish rendering of the name of the Byzantine village Angelokome; popularly explained by Turkish in "cave" and göl "lake"
column3: Angelokome, the castle of one of the first Byzantine lords (tekfurs) Osman Gazi fought, lay in the plain southeast of Uludağ; in Ottoman documents it was written Ezinegöl, then İnegöl. The people interpret the name as "lake with a cave"; this is a folk etymology. The İshak Pasha complex and the furniture industry define the town.

column2: Turkish ulu "lofty, great" + dağ "mountain"; ancient name Mysian Olympus, Ottoman name Keşiş Dağı (Monks' Mountain)
column3: The mountain rising to 2,543 meters above Bursa was known in antiquity as the Mysian Olympus; because of the monasteries on its slopes in the Byzantine period, the Ottomans called it Keşiş Dağı, "Monks' Mountain." In 1925 the name was changed to Uludağ, using the word ulu, from the Old Turkic root ulug, "great." Turkey's first ski resort was established here in the 1930s.

column2: From the name of the city of Adramyttion, founded by Adramys, son of the Lydian king Alyattes
column3: Adramyttion, founded by the Lydian prince Adramys, gave its name to the gulf at the foot of Mount Ida (Kaz Dağı); St. Paul's voyage to Rome began on a ship from this city. The Karesi principality took the city in the 14th century; in Turkish the form Edremid, then Edremit, became established. Olive oil production and the legends of Mount Ida define the region's identity.

column2: Greek pánormos "harbor offering shelter in every wind"
column3: The natural harbor beside Cyzicus bore the Greek name Panormos, "harbor fit for every ship"; the same name is the source of Palermo in Sicily. The town, Panderma in Ottoman documents and Bandırma in popular speech, is the largest port on the southern shore of the Marmara. The steamer that carried Mustafa Kemal to Samsun on May 19, 1919, bore this port's name.

column2: Turkish ayva "quince" + -lık, "quince orchard"; the Greek Kydonies has the same meaning (kydṓnion "quince")
column3: The town on the Aegean coast was known by the Greek name Kydonies, meaning "quince groves"; the Turkish name Ayvalık carries the same meaning, and the two names lived side by side for centuries. In the 18th century it grew rich on the olive oil trade as an autonomous Greek town; after the population exchange of 1923, Turks from Lesbos and Crete settled here. Cunda (Alibey) Island and Şeytan Sofrası are the town's landmarks.

column2: From the name of the Milesian colony Artake; the harbor on the south side of the Kapıdağ Peninsula
column3: Artake, founded by Milesians just west of Cyzicus, appears in Herodotus as a port of call of the Persian fleet. The town, which became the regional center after the destruction of Cyzicus, took the form Erdek in Turkish. The ruins of Cyzicus on the Kapıdağ Peninsula and the marble quarries of Marmara Island define the area.

column2: Turkish kapı "gate" + dağ "mountain": the mountainous peninsula standing like a gate onto the Marmara; its ancient name was Arktonnesos, "bear island"
column3: Known in antiquity as Arktonnesos, "bear island," it was an island settlement joined to the city of Cyzicus by two bridges; alluvial deposits attached it to the mainland and turned it into a peninsula. The Turks called the mountainous mass standing like a gate on the southern shore of the Marmara Kapıdağ. The Temple of Hadrian at Cyzicus was one of the largest temples of the ancient world.

column2: Greek mármaron "marble": from the island's famous white marble quarries; the Sea of Marmara also takes its name from here
column3: The ancient island of Proconnesus was the source of the white marble that adorned the palaces and churches of the Roman and Byzantine capital; the Greek word mármaron, "shining stone," became the name of the island and then of the whole sea. The Turkish word mermer, "marble," also entered from Greek. The marble quarries continued to be worked in the Ottoman period; Pîrî Reis charts the island under the name Marmara.

column2: Turkish rendering of the Byzantine Greek fortress name Tzouroulon; a Roman road station in Thrace
column3: Tzurulum, on the Roman road from Istanbul to Edirne, was one of the important fortresses of Thrace in the Byzantine period. The town, Çorlu in Turkish, joined the Ottoman realm in 1357; in 1511 the armies of Selim I (the Grim) and his father Bayezid II met here. It is one of the industrial centers of Thrace.

column2: Turkish burgaz, from Greek pýrgos "tower," + Persian lūle "pipe": "fortress with pipes," from meerschaum pipe bowls or water pipes
column3: The Thracian town known as Arkadioupolis after the emperor Arcadius bore the name Bergoule in the late Byzantine period; the Turkish word burgaz comes from Greek pýrgos, "tower, fortress." The word lüle was prefixed on account of the meerschaum pipe bowls (lüle) made in the town or the spouts of its fountains. The complex that Sokollu Mehmed Pasha commissioned from Mimar Sinan (1569) is the center of the town.

column2: City of Selys, with the Thracian element -bria "city": a settlement whose Thracian name was preserved by the Megarian colonists
column3: Selymbria, founded by the Megarians before Byzantion, carries the element -bria, meaning "city" in the Thracian language, and is linked by legend to the founder Selys; the same element appears in the name Mesembria (Nesebar). The town, Silivri in Ottoman times, became famous for its yogurt. The remains of the Byzantine walls and the Pîrî Mehmed Pasha Mosque are the town's historic buildings.

column2: Greek chēlḗ "claw, breakwater": from the claw-shaped rocky headland on the shore
column3: The fishing town on the Black Sea coast appears in the ancient Periplus texts under the name Chele; in Greek the word means both a crab's claw and a harbor breakwater, and describes the town's rocky headland. The lighthouse (1860) of the town, known in the Ottoman period for weaving Şile cloth, is one of the largest lighthouses in Turkey.

column2: Turkish ada "island" + pazar "market": from the marketplace set up on the island-like ground between the Sakarya and the Çark Suyu
column3: The fertile plain enclosed between the Sakarya River and the Çark Suyu, which flows out of Lake Sapanca, was an area that looked like an island; the town of Adapazarı developed around the marketplace established here in the 17th century. The word pazar comes from Persian bāzār. The city, center of the province of Sakarya founded in 1954, was heavily damaged in the earthquake of 1999.

column2: Turkish söğüt "willow tree": from the willow-grown area granted to Ertuğrul Gazi's Kayı tribe as winter quarters
column3: The Byzantine border town called Thebasion became Söğüt, which the Seljuk sultan granted to Ertuğrul Gazi as winter quarters; Osman Gazi's principality was born here. The word söğüt comes from Old Turkic sögüt and appears in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk. The tomb of Ertuğrul Gazi and the Yörük festivals held every year keep the memory of the founding alive.

column2: From the phrase "eis Nikomedeian" (to Nicomedia), the city founded by the Bithynian king Nicomedes I
column3: Nicomedia, founded by Nicomedes I in 264 BC, is the city Diocletian made the eastern capital of the Roman Empire; Hannibal died nearby and Constantine was baptized here. The Greek phrase "eis Nikomedeian" became İznikmid and then İzmit in Turkish; Orhan Gazi took the city in 1337. The Ottoman shipyard and the Pertev Pasha Mosque (by Mimar Sinan) are the city's Ottoman heritage.

column2: Greek chárax "palisaded wall, stockade": from the Byzantine stockade on the shore of the Gulf of İzmit
column3: Charax, mentioned by Procopius, was a Byzantine station on the shore of the gulf protected by a palisaded wall; its name turned into Hereke in Turkish. The silk carpets of the Hereke Imperial Factory, founded by Sultan Abdülmecid in 1843, furnished the Ottoman palaces; the Hereke carpet became a world brand.

column2: Turkish rendering of the Byzantine-era town name Dakibyza; neighbor of Libyssa, where Hannibal's tomb lay
column3: Dakibyza on the Marmara shore appears in Ottoman documents in the form Gekbüze and turned into Gebze in popular speech. Libyssa, where the Carthaginian commander Hannibal died in 183 BC, lies within the present-day borders of Gebze; the Çoban Mustafa Pasha complex (1523) is the town's Ottoman monument.

column2: From the name of Kara Mürsel Bey, the naval commander who founded Orhan Gazi's first Ottoman fleet
column3: The town on the southern shore of the Gulf of İzmit bears the name of Kara Mürsel Bey, who built up the first Ottoman naval force in the 1320s; the type of small warship named after him, the "karamürsel," lived on in Ottoman maritime vocabulary. Kara, meaning dark-skinned or strong in Turkish, was used as a nickname; Mürsel is Arabic for "one who is sent."

column2: Turkish uzun "long" + köprü "bridge": from the 174-arch stone bridge Murad II built over the Ergene River
column3: Between 1426 and 1443 Murad II built a stone bridge 1,392 meters long to cross the marshy Ergene valley; the town founded at the head of the bridge began under the name Ergene and was later called Uzunköprü after the bridge. The structure, considered the longest historic stone bridge in the world, is still in use. The word köprü comes from Old Turkic köprüg.

column2: From the name of the city of Ainos, mentioned by Homer in the Iliad; the harbor at the mouth of the Meriç (Maritsa)
column3: Ainos, where the Meriç empties into the Aegean, appears in Homer as a city of the Thracian allies and was refounded by Aeolian colonists in the 7th century BC. Mehmed II took it from the Genoese Gattilusio family in 1456; in Turkish it became Enez. The Byzantine fortress and the church of Hagia Sophia stand on the town's hill.

column2: From the name of Bizye, capital of the Thracian Astai tribe
column3: Bizye, at the foot of the Istranca Mountains, was the last capital of the Thracian kings and the seat of Thrace's local kings in the Roman period; the Byzantine church known as Little Hagia Sophia and an ancient theater stand in the town. The name, Vize in Turkish, is among the Thracian language's nearest witnesses to Anatolia.

column2: From the name Apaša, capital of Arzawa in Hittite texts; Greek Ephesos
column3: Apaša, which appears in Hittite documents as the capital of the kingdom of Arzawa in western Anatolia, was continued by Greek colonists under the name Ephesos. The Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the World; the Library of Celsus and the great theater are works of the Roman period. In Byzantine times the city was called Hagios Theologos after the church of St. John; the Turks rendered this as Ayasuluk. The form Efes is an adaptation of the Greek name into Turkish.

column2: From the name of the Seljuk dynasty; formerly Ayasuluk, from Greek Hagios Theologos, "the Holy Theologian (John)"
column3: The basilica that Justinian built over the tomb of St. John on the hill beside Ephesus was known by the Greek name Hagios Theologos, "the Holy Theologian"; the Turks adopted this as Ayasuluk, and the Aydınoğulları built the İsa Bey Mosque (1375) here. In 1914 the town was given the name of the Seljuk dynasty, which Turkified Anatolia. The name Selçuk comes from Selçuk Bey, the dynasty's ancestor.

column2: Greek pérgamon "citadel, high place" (a word of Anatolian origin); the word parchment derives from this city's name
column3: Pergamon, capital of the Attalid dynasty, was the cultural center of the Hellenistic world with its Altar of Zeus, its Asklepieion and its library of 200,000 scrolls. When Egypt cut off papyrus exports, the leather writing material developed here, "pergamenē," became the source of Latin pergamenum, French parchemin and Turkish parşömen. The city, Bergama in Turkish, is also famous for its carpet weaving.

column2: Turkish kuş "bird" + ada "island" + -sı: from the name of Güvercinada (Pigeon Island) in the harbor; the Genoese called it Scala Nova, "new quay"
column3: After the harbor of Ephesus silted up, Genoese and Venetian merchants founded a port in this bay under the name Scala Nova, "new quay"; the Ottomans took the area in 1413, and Öküz Mehmed Pasha built the caravanserai in 1618. The Turkish name comes from the small fortified island (Güvercinada) at the mouth of the harbor. The word kuş appears in the Orkhon Inscriptions in its Old Turkic form kuş.

column2: Persian çeşme "spring, fountain": from the freshwater springs on the shore; its ancient name was Kyssos
column3: The harbor opposite the island of Chios was in antiquity the landing of Kyssos, attached to Erythrai. The Turks named the town with the Persian-derived word çeşme because of the springs where sailors took on water; çeşme comes from Persian çeşm, "eye," and carries the sense of a spring. In the Battle of Çeşme of 1770 the Ottoman fleet was burned here; the Genoese castle was repaired by Bayezid.

column2: Greek phṓkē "seal": Phokaia, from the Mediterranean monk seals living in its bays
column3: The Ionian city of Phokaia was the home of the bold seafarers who founded Marseille (Massalia) and the colonies in Spain; its name comes from the seals that still live along its shores today. The town, the center of the Genoese alum trade in the 13th to 15th centuries, became Foça in Turkish. The Siren Rocks are associated with the sirens of Homer's Odyssey.

column2: Turkish rendering of Petronium, the Latin name of the Castle of St. Peter; popularly explained by Turkish bodrum, "cellar"
column3: On the ruins of ancient Halicarnassus the Knights of Rhodes built in 1402 a castle dedicated to St. Peter; the castle's Latin name, Petronium, turned into Bodrum in Turkish. Looking at the vaults among the ruins of the Mausoleum, the people explain the name with the Turkish word bodrum, "cellar"; this is a folk etymology. The Mausoleum, the monumental tomb in the city where Herodotus was born, was one of the Seven Wonders of the World. The Blue Voyage culture was born here in the 20th century.

column2: City name from the Carian language; capital of the Carian satrap Mausolus
column3: The city whose Carian name appears in Greek texts as Halikarnassos was the capital of the satrap Mausolus; his monumental tomb, the Mausoleion, gave the world's languages the word "mausoleum." Herodotus, the father of history, was born here. Alexander the Great besieged and took the city in 334 BC; its ruins lie beneath present-day Bodrum.

column2: Origin disputed; explained by Greek mármaron "marble" or (as a folk etymology) by the words "mimar as" ("hang the architect") attributed to Süleyman the Magnificent about the castle
column3: The town at the harbor of ancient Physkos appears in Ottoman documents in the form Mermeris; the name is associated with the Greek word for marble. Popular tradition holds that Süleyman the Magnificent, displeased with the castle during the Rhodes campaign of 1522, said "mimar as" ("hang the architect"); this is a folk etymology. The castle was built in 1522 as the base for the Rhodes campaign; the marina and pine forests are the town's present-day face.

column2: From the name of Fethi Bey, one of the first Turkish pilots, killed in 1914; Arabic fatḥ "conquest"; formerly Meğri (Greek Makri, "long")
column3: The Lycian city of Telmessos was famous for its oracles; the harbor, known in the Byzantine period as Makri, "long," became Meğri under the Ottomans. In 1934 the town was given the name of the pilot Fethi Bey, who died on the Istanbul-Cairo flight of 1914. The rock tombs and the Ölüdeniz lagoon are the town's landmarks; the Lycian form Telebehi appears in local inscriptions.

column2: Turkish rendering of the Byzantine-era harbor name Stadia; neighbor of ancient Knidos at the tip of the peninsula
column3: The harbor of Stadia in the middle of the Knidos peninsula appears in Byzantine sources; in Ottoman documents it took the form Dadya, and in popular speech Datça. Knidos, at the tip of the peninsula, was famous for the Aphrodite statue of Praxiteles and the observatory of Eudoxus. On the peninsula, known for its almond and honey production, blow the winds that Strabo also mentions.

column2: From the name of the city Millawanda (Milawata) in Hittite documents; Greek Miletos
column3: The harbor that appears in Hittite texts as Millawanda, attached to Ahhiyawa, became the most powerful city of the Ionian period; Thales, Anaximander and Hippodamus came from here. When the alluvium of the Menderes filled the harbor the city shrank; the Turks called the nearby village Balat, from the Greek palátion, "palace." The İlyas Bey Mosque (1404) is a work of the Menteşeoğulları.

column2: Greek dídymos "twin": from the oracle center of Didyma, dedicated to the twins Apollo and Artemis
column3: Didyma, at the end of the sacred way from Miletus, was the most famous Apollo oracle of the Greek world after Delphi; the columns of its giant temple still stand today. The Ottoman village bore the name Yoran; in the 1990s the town took Didim, the Turkified form of the ancient name. Altınkum beach is a tourist center.

column2: Turkish ala "variegated, reddish" + Persian şehir "city": the city at the foot of red-soiled hills; its ancient name was Philadelphia, "brotherly love"
column3: Philadelphia, founded by the Pergamene king Attalus II Philadelphus, is one of the seven churches in John's Book of Revelation, and its name, meaning brotherly love, also inspired Philadelphia in the United States. The Turks called the city Alaşehir because of its reddish hills. As Byzantium's last stronghold in Anatolia it held out until 1390; it is famous for its sultana grapes.

column2: From the Lydian city name Sfard; capital of the Lydian Kingdom, the city where coinage was invented
column3: Sardis, capital of the Lydian king Croesus, struck the world's first coins from the gold in the alluvium of the Pactolus (Sart Çayı); the Turkish expression "as rich as Karun" comes from this king's name. The name, Sfard in Lydian inscriptions, became Sardeis in Greek; it was the western terminus of the Persian Royal Road. The remains of the Temple of Artemis and the synagogue lie beside the village of Sart.

column2: Turkish ak "white" + Arabic hisar "fortress": from the fortress of white stone; its ancient name was Thyateira
column3: Thyateira, one of the seven churches of Revelation, was a Lydian city famous for its guild of dyers. In the period of the Saruhanoğulları the Turks called the white-stone fortress Akhisar; the word hisar comes from Arabic ḥiṣār, "siege, fortress." Tobacco and olive growing are the town's economy.

column2: Turkish rendering of the Byzantine-era town name Teira; the Aydınoğlu center in the Küçük Menderes plain
column3: Teira, on the southern edge of the Küçük Menderes plain, was a bishopric in the Byzantine period. The Aydınoğulları took and developed the city in the 14th century; Timur wintered here in 1402. Tire was known in the Ottoman period for its felt and weaving crafts, and today for its Tuesday market.

column2: From the Turkish personal name Ötemiş (öte- "to pay a debt, to fulfill"); the name of a Turkmen bey who settled in the region
column3: The town at the foot of Bozdağ is called after a bey named Ötemiş who settled in the region in the period of the Aydınoğulları; this personal name, derived from the Old Turkic verb öte-, turned into ödemiş in Turkish. Nearby Birgi was the capital of Aydınoğlu Mehmed Bey. Ödemiş potatoes and the Bozdağ highland pasture are the town's landmarks.

column2: From the name of the Phrygian city Kadoi; the Gediz River (ancient Hermos) also takes its name from this town
column3: The Phrygian city of Kadoi lay in the source region of the Hermos River; the town's name, Gediz in Turkish, also became the source of the river's Turkish name. The ancient Hermos is the river that carries the gold-bearing Pactolus tributary of Sardis. After the earthquake of 1970 the town was relocated to a new site.

column2: Turkish pamuk "cotton" + kale "castle": from likening the white travertines to heaps of cotton and the ancient city on the hilltop to a castle
column3: The white travertines formed over thousands of years by calcium-rich hot springs were likened by the Turks to heaps of cotton; the ruins of Hierapolis, "holy city," on the hilltop were taken for a castle. Hierapolis, founded by the kings of Pergamon, was famous for its thermal baths and the tomb of St. Philip. The word pamuk comes from Persian panbe. It is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

column2: City of Laodike, from the name of Laodike, wife of the Seleucid king Antiochus II
column3: In the 3rd century BC Antiochus II founded in the Lykos valley the city bearing the name of his wife Laodike; the city, which grew rich on the wool trade and banking, is one of the seven churches of Revelation. The Seljuks called the city Lâdik; Denizli was founded in its place. The stadium and theaters uncovered in excavations reflect the Roman period.

column2: City of Aphrodite, from the name of the goddess; the Ottoman village Geyre is a remnant of the name Caria
column3: The city in the interior of Caria won fame in the Roman period for its cult of Aphrodite and its school of marble sculpture; the Sebasteion reliefs and the stadium are extraordinarily well preserved. The settlement, renamed Stauropolis, "city of the cross," in Byzantine times, lived on in the Ottoman village of Geyre; the name Geyre is a trace of the regional name Caria.

column2: The city name Mylasa, from the Carian language; the first capital of Caria, sanctuary of Zeus Karios
column3: Mylasa, the capital of the Carian satraps before Halicarnassus, was the religious center of the region with its sanctuary of Zeus Karios and Labraunda; Strabo describes the city's wealth in marble. The town, center of the Menteşeoğulları principality, became Milas in Turkish; the Firuz Bey Mosque (1394) and the Gümüşkesen monumental tomb show two eras side by side. Milas carpets are famous.

column2: Turkish karşı "opposite" + yaka "shore": the opposite shore of the gulf as seen from the center of İzmir; its Greek name was Kordelio
column3: The Greek and Levantine summer resort on the northern shore of the Gulf of İzmir was known by the name Kordelio; the Turks called it Karşıyaka because it lay on the shore of the gulf opposite the city center. The word yaka means "edge, shore" in Old Turkic. The grave of Atatürk's mother Zübeyde Hanım is here.

column2: Turkish al "red" + sancak "banner": from the Turkish flag planted here at the liberation; formerly Punta, Italian for "point"
column3: The Levantine quarter on the point jutting into the gulf was known as Punta, from the Italian word punta, "point." In memory of the Turkish flag planted here at the liberation of İzmir on September 9, 1922, the district took the name Alsancak. The word sancak comes from the Old Turkic root sanç-, "to thrust in"; al is an old Turkic color term meaning "red."

column2: Turkish kadife "velvet" (Arabic qaṭīfa) + kale "castle": from the soft-looking walls of the Hellenistic fortress on the hill of Pagos
column3: On the hill of Pagos, which Alexander the Great is said to have seen in a dream, Lysimachus founded the new fortress of İzmir; in the Ottoman period the fortress was called Kadifekale because its walls looked as soft as velvet. The word kadife comes from Arabic qaṭīfa. The fortress is a vantage point commanding the gulf.

column2: City name from the Carian language; the Ionian city where Hippodamus's grid plan was applied
column3: Priene, at the foot of Mount Mykale, is a model Ionian city rebuilt on a grid plan in the 4th century BC; its Temple of Athena was built by Alexander the Great. Bias, one of the Seven Sages, came from here. The Ottomans called the Byzantine fortress beside the city Samsun Kalesi; the ancient name passed into Turkish as Priene.

column2: City of Antiochus, from the name of Antiochus, father of Seleucus I
column3: In 300 BC Seleucus I Nicator founded on the banks of the Orontes (Asi) the capital bearing the name of his father Antiochus; Antioch, the third-largest city of Rome, is the place where Christians were first given the name "Christian." The Arabic pronunciation Anṭākiya became Antakya in Turkish; the city passed through the Crusader Principality, Mamluk and Ottoman periods. The Church of St. Peter and the mosaic museum are the city's ancient heritage.

column2: Arabic rendering of Alexandreia, founded by Alexander the Great after his victory at Issus; İskender is Arabic al-Iskandar
column3: After defeating the Persian king Darius at Issus in 333 BC, Alexander the Great founded a harbor bearing his own name at the head of the gulf in memory of the victory. The name, al-Iskandarūn in Arabic, became İskenderun in Turkish; in Western languages it is called Alexandretta, "little Alexandria." It was the Ottoman port opening onto Aleppo; the iron and steel works and the naval base are its present-day identity.

column2: Mountain of St. Simeon (Samân): from the hilltop monastery of the monk Simeon Stylites, who lived on top of a pillar
column3: On the mountain near Seleucia Pieria, the port of Antioch, stood the monastery of Simeon Stylites the Younger, who lived on top of a pillar in the 6th century; the mountain was called after this saint, and the Arabic form Samʿān turned into Saman in Turkish. The town, Süveydiye in Ottoman times, became Samandağ in 1948; the Tunnel of Titus is a monument of Roman engineering.

column2: Arabic ḥarbiyya "pertaining to war": from the military unit stationed here in the Ottoman period; its ancient name was Daphne, "laurel"
column3: Daphne, the summer retreat of Antioch, was held to be the place where the nymph Daphne, pursued by Apollo, turned into a laurel tree; it was famous for its waterfalls and its temple of Apollo. The Arabs called it Bayt al-Māʾ, "house of water," for its abundant springs. The name Harbiye took hold in the late Ottoman period with the stationing of military units; the production of laurel soap keeps the ancient name alive.

column2: From the name of the Seljuk sultan Alâeddin Keykubad, with the Arabic adjectival form ʿAlāʾiyya, "belonging to Alâeddin"; Alanya since 1935
column3: Korakesion, a refuge of pirates, bore the name Kalonoros, "beautiful mountain," in the Byzantine period because of its rocky headland. Alâeddin Keykubad took the fortress in 1221 and built the shipyard and the Red Tower; the city became Alâiye after his name. In 1935, during Atatürk's visit, the form that appeared in the writing of a telegram was adopted and the name was made Alanya. The Seljuk shipyard is the only preserved medieval shipyard in the Mediterranean.

column2: Pomegranate in the indigenous Anatolian language of Side: the city's coins bear the pomegranate as an emblem
column3: Side on the Pamphylian coast is known for its people, who spoke an Anatolian language of their own, and for its pre-Greek inscriptions; its name means "pomegranate" in Sidetic, and the pomegranate was the city's emblem. It was famous for its Roman slave market and its Temple of Apollo. The village of Selimiye, founded by Cretan immigrants in the 19th century, stands on top of the ruins.

column2: Turkish rendering of a settlement name going back to the Luwian period; the ancient name of the Manavgat River was Melas, "black"
column3: The Manavgat River, descending from the Taurus, bore the name Melas, "black river," in antiquity; the town's name, on the other hand, is traced to a settlement name surviving from the Luwian period. The town, which appears in Ottoman documents in the form Manavgat, lies right beside Side; it is known for its waterfall and the Oymapınar Dam.

column2: Turkish kaş "eyebrow-shaped shore, slope": from the steep eyebrow-like slope behind the town; its ancient name was Antiphellos
column3: The Lycian city of Antiphellos appears in Lycian inscriptions as Habesos; the town, called Andifli in Ottoman documents, was named Kaş because of the steep slope descending to the sea like an eyebrow. In Old Turkic the word kaş means both the eyebrow above the eye and "mountain slope, edge." The Lycian sarcophagi and the harbor facing the island of Meis (Kastellorizo) are the town's landmarks.

column2: Turkish rendering of the name of the Lycian city Myra (Dembre > Demre); the city of Santa Claus (St. Nicholas)
column3: Myra, a leading city of the Lycian League, is the city of St. Nicholas (Santa Claus), who served as its bishop in the 4th century; its rock tombs and theater are famous. The name, which took the form Dembre and then Demre in Turkish, appeared in official documents as Kale until 2005. Greenhouse tomatoes and the Church of St. Nicholas are the town's two faces.

column2: Greek Phoinike "Phoenicia": the harbor founded by Phoenician merchants; phoînix also means the date palm
column3: The harbor on the Lycian coast bore the name Phoinike because the Phoenicians founded it as a trading base; the Greek word phoînix means both Phoenician and date palm, and both meanings fit the town. The ancient cities of Limyra and Arykanda lie nearby; orange groves are the town's present-day emblem.

column2: Persian kamar "belt, arch": from the arch-shaped stone embankment built along the foot of the mountain to hold back floodwaters
column3: The arch-shaped stone embankment, kilometers long, built above the village in 1916–1917 to protect it from the floodwaters coming down from the Beydağları gave Eski Köy its new name. The word kemer passed into Turkish from Persian kamar, "belt." The ruins of ancient Phaselis and Olympos lie within the district; it became a tourist center after the 1980s.

column2: Name of the three-harbored Lycian city founded by Rhodian colonists; associated with Greek phásēlos, "bean"
column3: Phaselis, founded by Rhodian colonists in the 7th century BC, was a Lycian city that traded in rose oil and timber through its three natural harbors; Alexander the Great spent a winter here. The name is said to be connected with the Greek word phásēlos, "bean; light boat." The ruins lie today in the pine forest near Tekirova.

column2: City name from the Pisidian language; the eagle's-nest city that Alexander the Great gave up besieging
column3: Termessos, 1,000 meters up on Güllük Dağı, was the city of the mountain people mentioned by Homer, whom the Pisidians called the Solymi. Alexander the Great besieged the city in 333 BC but moved on without taking it. Its theater, agora and sarcophagi are preserved on the mountaintop; the Pisidian name was transmitted by Greek authors.

column2: From the name of the city Parha in Hittite documents; the center of the Artemis cult in Pamphylia
column3: The city that appears as Parha in a treaty of the Hittite king Tudhaliya IV became the capital of Pamphylia in the Greek period under the name Perge; it was famous for its temple of Artemis Pergaia and its stadium. The mathematician Apollonius was born here; St. Paul visited the city on his first journey. The ruins lie beside the town of Aksu.

column2: From Estwediya, the city's native name on its coins; associated with the name of the Late Hittite king Azatiwada
column3: Aspendos, on the banks of the Köprüçay, used the name Estwediya on its own coins; this name is associated with Azatiwada in the Karatepe inscriptions. Its Roman theater (2nd century AD) is the best-preserved ancient theater in the world; the local people call the theater Belkıs Sarayı, the Palace of Belkıs (the Queen of Sheba). Its aqueducts are an example of Roman engineering.

column2: Korkut's land, from the name of Prince Korkut, son of Bayezid II and governor of the sanjak of Teke
column3: The town on the site of the Pisidian city of Isinda bore the name İstanoz under the Ottomans. In 1926 the town was given the name of the poet-prince Korkut, who served as governor of the sanjak in Antalya at the beginning of the 16th century; Korkut is an old Turkic personal name that also lives on in the name Dede Korkut. The Alâeddin Mosque and the Sinaneddin Madrasa are Seljuk works.

column2: From the name of the city Tarša in Hittite texts; capital of Cilicia, birthplace of St. Paul
column3: Tarsus, which appears in Hittite documents as the city of Tarša in Kizzuwatna, is mentioned in the Assyrian annals under the name Tarzi. Cleopatra and Antony met here; St. Paul was born in this city. The Arabic pronunciation Ṭarsūs remained unchanged in Turkish. The Great Mosque from the period of the Ramazanoğulları and Cleopatra's Gate are the city's monuments; the mound of Gözlükule reaches back to the Bronze Age.

column2: City of Seleucus, from the name of Seleucus I Nicator; Seleucia on the Kalykadnos (Göksu)
column3: In the 3rd century BC Seleucus I founded on the banks of the Göksu the city bearing his own name; the German emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned in this river in 1190 during the Third Crusade. The Arabic form Salūqiya became Silifke in Turkish; the Karamanoğulları and Ottoman fortress stands on the town's hill. The region is also remembered through the folk song "Silifke'nin yoğurdu" (Silifke's yogurt).

column2: Greek ánemos "wind" + oúrion "cape": "windy cape"; the southernmost tip of Anatolia
column3: Anemourion, on the cape that is Turkey's southernmost point, takes its name from its windy position facing Cyprus; its Roman-period necropolis and baths are preserved on the slope of the cape. Mamure Castle of the Karamanoğulları is one of the sturdiest medieval castles on the coast. Banana growing is the town's present-day emblem.

column2: Arabic Jayḥān: the name of the Pyramos River, which Islamic geographers identified with the Ceyhun (Oxus), one of the rivers of paradise
column3: The Pyramos River, which waters the eastern Çukurova, was counted by Arab geographers among the rivers flowing out of paradise, like the Ceyhun (Amu Darya) in Central Asia, and was called Jayḥān; in the same way the Saros was named Seyhan. The river's name was given in the 1920s to the town of Hamidiye, founded in the 19th century. The port of Yumurtalık and Yılankale lie within the district's borders.
